lines: Seven. Warren G. Harding. The Turkey In The Aviation Helmet.
The 1920s were a strange time for turkeys.
In 1921, a turkey named Supreme the Second was flown to the White House for Harding.
He wore an aviation helmet and goggles.
According to the Baltimore Sun, he was also "clad in a black and gold sweater held on by a pink bow."
The flight ended early.
The turkey got airsick.
He finished the trip by train.
The next year, a club in Chicago sent Supreme the Third.
He had been fattened on chocolates.
He travelled more than 800 miles by road in under 38 hours, in a cage hung on springs.
A special motor coat was made for him.
Was Supreme spared?
The record doesn't say.
He did get a sweater.
Eight. Calvin Coolidge. The Raccoon.
Back to our cold open.
Calvin Coolidge did not like people sending him food.
The New York Times reported he did not think the practice should "be encouraged."
People sent it anyway.
Quail.
Ducks.
Geese.
Rabbits.
Once, a deer.
And in November 1926, a supporter from Nitta Yuma, Mississippi, sent a live raccoon.
With the suggestion that it be "served up for Thanksgiving dinner."
It was said to have a "toothsome flavor."
Coolidge had never eaten raccoon.
He was not about to start.
Instead, the family kept her.
For Christmas, she got her name, Rebecca, and an embroidered collar that read "White House Raccoon."
Rebecca walked on a leash.
She lived in a little house on the grounds.
First Lady Grace Coolidge carried her at the 1927 Easter Egg Roll and let children pet her.
Mrs.
Coolidge later said Rebecca's favourite pastime was "playing in a partly filled bathtub with a cake of soap."
Then the White House got her a companion.
A male raccoon, caught in northern Virginia.
His name was Horace.
The President renamed him Reuben.
Reuben and Rebecca did not get along.
Reuben escaped.
Repeatedly.
Once he stopped traffic on Pennsylvania Avenue for 30 minutes.
Eventually, he left for good.
When the Coolidges left in 1929, Rebecca went to the zoo in Rock Creek Park, to live with other raccoons.
Scoreboard: Turkeys spared, one, asterisk.
Raccoons spared: one.
No asterisk.
Nine. Franklin D. Roosevelt. Franksgiving.
Now we get to the calendar crisis.
In 1939, November had five Thursdays.
The last Thursday fell on November 30th.
The very last day of the month.
Retailers panicked.
A late Thanksgiving meant a short Christmas shopping season.
And the economy was still recovering from the Great Depression.
So FDR moved Thanksgiving.
One week earlier, to November 23rd.
The country did not take it well.
Critics called it "Franksgiving."
One calendar maker said the change made his calendars "obsolete."
Football coaches complained: big games were scheduled for the old date.
And the states could not agree.
In 1939, twenty-two states followed the President, and celebrated on November 23rd.
Twenty-three stuck with November 30th.
And three states, Texas, Colorado and Mississippi, celebrated both.
Two Thanksgivings.
Excellent.
In 1940, FDR did it again.
Sixteen states ignored him again.
A New York City survey of store owners found no real sales boost.
So in May 1941, Roosevelt said the holiday would go back to the last Thursday of November.
Congress went one better.
The House passed a resolution for the last Thursday.
The Senate changed it to the fourth Thursday, so the date would stay put in years with five Thursdays.
And on December 26th, 1941, Roosevelt signed it into law.
That's why Thanksgiving is the fourth Thursday of November today.
Because of a shopping argument.
In 1942, during the Second World War, FDR read his proclamation over the radio.
Dinner that year: clam cocktail, roast turkey with chestnut stuffing, and pumpkin pie with cheese.
Pumpkin pie with cheese.
We'll allow it.
It was wartime.
